column1: # Why each repository of the pool is in the Design Studio pool.
# `owner/name<TAB>the reason` - one line per repository. The table in
# which joins this file with `docs/design/evidence/github-repos-<date>.tsv`, so
# the numbers in the document cannot drift away from the API.
# The file is read in the order of the categories of the document.
# --- A. React Native design systems and UI kits ---------------------------

column2: Compile-time token flattening and a shared web/native token model - the one idea worth stealing from a kit we do not adopt.
The only RN kit that shipped real accessibility work in 2026 (accessible modals, portal AT hiding, reduce-motion forwarding).
Theming and a codemod layer; a good example of a kit with one maintainer and a multi-package release train.
A long-lived kit with a real screen gallery - the closest thing the RN world has to a visual reference library.
The only kit that ships both a NativeWind and a Unistyles-adjacent variant of every component, and it added reduced motion in 2026.
A 2025 kit on the newest stack, but it depends on NativeWind and expo-blur - both barred by our rules.
The most-starred RN kit and the classic answer: the proof that popularity is not maintenance.
The best accessibility primitives in the pool and the proof that a Tailwind-shaped system cannot sit on our token source.
The pager every RN app used, archived in 2022: what happens to a library the community stops paying for.
The modern tab bar with an animated shared indicator - the one piece of the tab bar we may want.
Theming without a CSS runtime: the theme object is a plain object, like ours.

column1: # --- B. Styling engines, tokens and colour ---------------------------------

column2: Our styling engine: the only one that keeps the tokens as plain TypeScript and needs no build step.
The credible NativeWind replacement: Tailwind v4 in RN with a Metro transform worker.
The industry token pipeline; our token package is written as if it were built by it, so we should know what it would change.
Reference accessible colour scales - a check on our hand-rolled 50-950 ramp.
The source of the Material Symbols we use as the one icon set of the product.
Our motion engine: the only one that runs on the UI thread and keeps the frame budget.
The runtime Reanimated 4 runs on; the separate repository is a placeholder, which is a lesson in reading the README.
The declarative Reanimated wrapper most people reach for first - and the example of a big install base with no release since 2025.
The vector engine for custom work: shaders, blur and gradients - most of which our own rules forbid.
The same project under the name npm still installs from; the naming history is a maintenance warning.
The design-file animation runtime: the benchmark for "a picture of an animation" against a real interaction.
The Android runtime of the same, and the origin of the Lottie file format.
Interactive vector animation with a state machine: the only one of the two that can respond to a delivery.
The web motion standard; it is what the web dashboard should feel like, and it has dropped RN support.
The reference animation toolbox - helpers worth reading, a dependency we should not take.
Platform-native animations with no JS overhead, from a maintainer we already depend on.
Rolling counters: exactly the "stops remaining" number, if we ever want it to roll.
A declarative animation API with a NativeWind peer dependency - barred, but a useful reference.
A real Reanimated 4 carousel: the shape of the onboarding carousel we may want.
A 2026 animation library with no release and no licence file - the two failures that kill a dependency.
The haptic patterns of the platform behind one API; our confirm/deliver/error language belongs here.

column1: # --- D. Sheets, gestures, lists and shared elements ------------------------

column2: Our gesture engine: gestures are recognised on the UI thread, which is the basis of the no-jank budget.
The incumbent sheet: 11.9 million downloads a month and no commit since May 2026.
The 2026 challenger: a Fabric sheet with a critically damped spring on both platforms, by construction.
The best-maintained sheet in the pool: twelve releases in six months and two open issues.
The classic long-press drag list, built on the Reanimated 2 API.
Drag-and-drop reorder for Reanimated 4 - the shape of "voice plus drag" for the route editor.
A small, active reorderable list with a stable API.
The swipe-to-reveal row every delivery app copies, including ours.
A Fabric list with three hundred commits in ninety days and no release since 2024.
Pinch and zoom on Reanimated - the map gesture, if we need our own.
The classic modal sheet with drag-to-dismiss, dormant since 2024.
The original Reanimated sheet, superseded by gorhom's.

column1: # --- E. Icons, fonts, accessibility and the platform ------------------------

column2: The single Material Symbols source - our one-icon-set rule.
The vector layer under any custom icon or route ribbon.
The Figtree source: our type face, licensed OFL.
The font repository itself, and the licence file every app store asks about.
Screen-reader helpers for React Native: announcements, focus order, focus trapping.
Explicit focus order and focus trapping on Android and iOS.
The lint rules for accessibility that our ESLint config does not have yet.
The accessibility engine of the web; there is no React Native package for it, which is the reason our a11y gate is a manual review.
The list that keeps 300 stops at 60 fps; Expo SDK 58 bundles it.
The navigator we build on.
The insets of the device, and the layout of every screen that has to clear the notch.
Fast storage for the offline queue; the New Architecture bridge under it.
The native-module bridge Unistyles 3 and MMKV sit on.
The localisation layer, and the right-to-left dependency behind the Arabic build.

column1: # --- F. Maps, map styling and the routing we draw on ----------------------

column2: The map engine of the app: it draws our own style, offline, with no proprietary SDK.
The same engine for the web: one style spec, one colour system, two platforms.
The style spec itself - the contract between our palette and the map.
The editor for the style: the way the courier map style is built and reviewed.
The basemap style we build the Canterbury pack from, and the reference for "a map that reads in daylight".
The tile format of the offline pack.
A tile server that renders any vector style; the way the style is published.
A complete GL style: the fastest way to read how a good map style is put together.
The vector tile schema our style is built on.
The proprietary engine we do not use; archived, and the reason the licence of the map SDK matters.
The tool that answers "is this address in OSM", used by the address engine.
The routing engine behind the road geometry of the day.
The routing engine that handles the vehicle profile and the turn-by-turn.
The routing and the isochrones for the "is it worth walking" decisions; GPL, so clean-room only.

column1: # --- G. The open-source work of the reference products ---------------------

column2: What a bank publishes about its own API: the plainest possible product language.
GitHub's design system: how a large product documents its components and its motion.
The Fluent design language in code: the density and the keyboard rules of a desktop tool.
The accessibility-first component library: the reference for focus behaviour.
A complete open-source design system with a documented scale and a dark mode done properly.
The Tailwind-era system: what "a component library" means in 2026.
The dashboard density that an operations screen should never reach - and the boundary we must not cross.
The charting library for the earnings and the end-of-day card.
The platform we build on: the SDK 58 bundle table that decides what we can use.
